authoredSolutions.73: Tangent to \(y^{2}=24x\) at \((6t^{2},12t)\) is \(ty=x+6t^{2}\). It meets \(xy=2\) where \(ty^{2}-6t^{2}y-2=0\), so for \(A,B\): \(y_{1}+y_{2}=6t,\ y_{1}y_{2}=-\frac{2}{t}\). The midpoint \(M\) has \(y_{M}=3t\) and \(x_{M}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2}{y_{1}}+\frac{2}{y_{2}}\right)=\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{y_{1}y_{2}}=-3t^{2}\). Eliminating \(t\) gives the locus \(y^{2}=-3x\), a parabola with latus rectum \(3\) and directrix \(x=\frac{3}{4}\), i.e. \(4x=3\).
authoredSolutions.80: Two edge vectors of the plane are \((-3,4,-3)\) and \((1,-1,1)\); their cross product gives the normal \((1,0,-1)\), so the plane is \(x-z-1=0\). The distance of \((7,-3,-4)\) is \(\frac{|7-(-4)-1|}{\sqrt{1^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}=\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}=5\sqrt{2}\).
authoredSolutions.98: [Textbook answer-key note: the source keys 45 V and its solution reasons "resistances are same so equal division of potential", which treats the voltmeter as IDEAL and discards the stated \(400\Omega\). A real voltmeter loads the circuit: \(100\Omega\) in parallel with \(400\Omega\) is \(80\Omega\), so the total becomes \(180\Omega\), \(I = 90/180 = 0.5\text{ }A\) and the meter reads \(0.5 \times 80 = 40\text{ }V\) — option D, and the reason the \(400\Omega\) is given at all. 45 V follows only if the meter is ideal, or if two meters are used simultaneously (one across each resistor), which the singular "A voltmeter" does not describe. The official key is preserved here to match the board.] Treating the voltmeter as ideal, the two equal resistors divide the emf equally: \(V = \frac{90}{2} = 45\text{ }V\).
authoredSolutions.165: \(A\) lies on the \(y\)-axis, which forces \((\lambda-2)^{2}=0\), so \(\lambda=2\), giving \(A(0,2)\), \(AB:3x+2y=4\) and \(AC:y=2x+2\). With orthocentre \((1,2)\), the altitude from \(A\) is \(y=2\) and the altitude from \(C\) (slope \(\frac{2}{3}\)) meets \(AC\) at \(C\left(-\frac{1}{2},1\right)\). A tangent from \(C\) to \(y^{2}=6x\) touches the first-quadrant branch at \(\left(\frac{3}{2},3\right)\), so its length is \(\sqrt{2^{2}+2^{2}}=2\sqrt{2}\).
authoredSolutions.169: The \(5\)-digit numbers use all digits: \(5!=120\), and each exceeds \(7000\). A \(4\)-digit number exceeds \(7000\) only when its leading digit is \(7\) or \(8\): \(2\times P(4,3)=2\times24=48\). Total \(=120+48=168\).
